lines: A model's offline score was reported six months ago from a dataset nobody can rebuild today.
The tables underneath have since been compacted, and whoever ran that original query never saved it anywhere.
Same query, run again right now, would return something different, and nothing about running it warns you of that.
Two different tools exist for exactly this problem, built at two very different scales.
One is meant for branching an entire derived dataset inside a data lake. The other is meant for pinning a single file that sits right next to your training script.
Which one actually fits a dataset the size you're building right now?
answer: It isn't a matter of taste between two interchangeable tools.
A dataset the size of a whole derived table belongs with the lake-scale tool. A single file tracked alongside your code belongs with the file-scale one. Scale decides it, not preference.

lines: Querying the current table means querying something that keeps moving underneath you.
A snapshot or a tag works completely differently: it's a name pointing at one exact state of the data, fixed the moment it was created.
Point a query at that name instead, and nothing happening to the live table afterward can change what it returns.
Here's what a branch actually is under the hood.
It's a pointer aimed at one commit, plus whatever changes haven't been committed yet. Creating it duplicates nothing at all.
A tag does something simpler still: it just gives one specific commit a name you can come back to later.
Neither of those two things touches a single byte of the underlying data when it's created.
A completely different tool identifies a file by the hash of its contents, not by its name or where it sits.
Two files holding identical bytes land on the exact same hash, no matter what either one is called, and get stored once instead of twice.
Change even one byte inside that file, and the hash changes with it, every time.
Put the two mechanisms next to the two problems they were each built for.
A whole derived dataset inside a lake gets the branch: an isolated view you can build on and merge once it's validated.
A single file sitting beside your training script gets the content pin: a hash that travels along with the exact Git commit of the code that produced it.
Neither tool is better in general. Each one is simply built for its own scale.
None of this proves anything about which model actually trained on which data unless something writes that link down.
An experiment tracker's logged-model record does exactly that: it ties one model run to the exact dataset digest it trained on and the exact code commit that produced it, in a single entry.
Give that entry a name when you log it, and later you can search back through every run by the dataset that trained it.
A label is not a fixed fact sitting quietly in a column. It has its own definition, and that definition can change.
Widen or narrow the window that counts as a churn, and the exact same customer rows, with the exact same feature values, suddenly carry a different answer.
Pinning the features alone was never the whole job. If the label's own definition moved, calling it the same training set is already wrong.
Put the whole shape back together.
Query a snapshot or a tag, never the current table as it happens to look right now. Pick the versioning tool by the scale of what you're actually pinning.
Link the dataset, the code and the model together in one tracked record. And keep an eye on the label's own version, not only the data feeding it.
Skip any one of those four and the rest stop meaning what you think they mean.
Picture a team that calls itself reproducible because it re-runs the exact same SQL query against its live tables every quarter.
No snapshot anywhere in that process. No tag. Just the same text, sent again and again.
Does running an unchanged query count as reproducing an unchanged dataset?
answer: A query is only ever as stable as whatever it happens to be reading.
Without something pinning the source tables in place, the exact same query keeps quietly returning a different dataset every single time the tables underneath it move.
